title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro apps: Word, Lightroom, Blender and more are getting touch support
summary: Touchscreen MacBook Pro apps: Word, Lightroom, Blender and more are getting touch support
detailed: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is the first Mac you can touch, and Apple has lined up a list of named apps built to take advantage of it.

sentences: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is the first Mac you can touch, and Apple has lined up a list of named apps built to take advantage of it.
The laptop starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch, with preorders open now and arrivals from Friday, November 6.
The full app list is in Apple’s announcement , but one footnote changes how you should read it.
Apple grouped the third-party apps by the kind of work they do.

That’s a broad spread, from office documents and video calls to sculpting and DJ software.
ZBrush and Shapr3D are an interesting pair, since both are tools where you shape things by hand, and both already have touch-first versions on iPad.

Apple says the apps listed will be available later this year.
In other words, the optimized touch versions of these apps aren’t promised for November 6 when the first machines arrive.
Apple gave no dates for individual apps, so expect them to roll out over the coming weeks rather than all at once.
You won’t be stuck in the meantime.
Apple says many existing apps work with touch right away because macOS translates touches into clicks.
So you can tap buttons and menus in apps that haven’t been updated.
You just won’t get the custom gestures and controls the named developers are building.

Apple says its own apps are optimized for the new MacBook Pro, and it called out three Apple Creator Studio apps with specific touch features:
Logic Pro’s keyboard is the most practical example here.
If you sketch musical ideas on a plane or in a hotel room, playing chords on the display beats clicking notes in one at a time.
Final Cut Pro’s pinch to zoom is the kind of small change you’ll likely use dozens of times per edit.

The release also shows other pro apps running on the new MacBook Pro, including Cinema 4D, MATLAB, Nuke, LM Studio and TouchDesigner, with Redshift, Blender and Unreal Engine named for GPU performance.
Apple shows those for speed, though, and doesn’t list all of them as touch-optimized.
For developers, Apple says it has updated its system gesture APIs so apps can offer experiences designed specifically for touch.
That’s how the named apps above will go beyond simple tap-to-click.
Apple also says developers can test how touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.
That should help the many iPhone and iPad apps that already run on Apple silicon Macs, since developers can check touch behaviour on real Mac hardware.
Apple hadn’t posted a separate developer news item about Mac touch on developer.apple.com at the time of writing, so details such as the exact API names and the Xcode version needed weren’t public.
We’ll update this when Apple publishes developer documentation.
If your daily work lives in Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro or Pixelmator Pro, you get Apple’s touch features with Apple’s own apps, and the case for buying now is strong.
The same goes if you mostly need tap-to-click in apps you already own.
If you’re buying mainly for touch in Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender or Office, you’re relying on a “later this year” promise with no dates.
The MacBook Pro is a strong machine without them, but if touch support in one of those apps is your deciding factor, it costs you nothing to wait until the update ships and see how well it works.
Apple takes orders for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display on its online store and in the Apple Store app, and it ships November 6.
If you don’t need touch, Amazon has the M5 Pro and M5 Max models it sits beside for up to $610 off.
